meta.pageTitle: GATE CSE Operating Systems Previous Year Questions - Solved PYQs

questions.text:
[latex]P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\} [/latex] consists of all active processes in an operating system. [latex]R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\} [/latex] consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system.
The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

[latex] \text{Assignment edges: } R_1 \to P_1, R_2 \to P_2, R_3 \to P_3, R_4 \to P_4 [/latex] (the assignment edge [latex]R_1 \to P_1[/latex] means resource [latex]R_1[/latex] is assigned to process [latex]P_1[/latex], and so on for others)

[latex] \text{Claim edges: } P_1 \to R_2, P_2 \to R_3, P_3 \to R_1, P_2 \to R_4, P_4 \to R_2 [/latex] (the claim edge [latex]P_1 \to R_2[/latex] means process [latex]P_1[/latex] is waiting for resource [latex]R_2[/latex], and so on for others)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Build the resource-allocation graph and look for cycles (with single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock):

Cycle A: [latex]P_1\to R_2\to P_2\to R_3\to P_3\to R_1\to P_1[/latex] (involving [latex]P_1,P_2,P_3[/latex]).
Cycle B: [latex]P_2\to R_4\to P_4\to R_2\to P_2[/latex] (involving [latex]P_2,P_4[/latex]).

Both cycles share [latex]P_2[/latex] as a common process. Aborting [latex]P_2[/latex] alone breaks both cycles simultaneously (removing [latex]P_2[/latex]'s edges collapses both cycles at once) — system becomes deadlock-free.

Aborting [latex]P_1[/latex] alone only breaks Cycle A; Cycle B (which never involved [latex]P_1[/latex]) remains fully intact — still deadlocked. Similarly, aborting [latex]P_3[/latex] alone only touches Cycle A, leaving Cycle B untouched — still deadlocked.

Aborting both [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] together: removing [latex]P_1[/latex] frees [latex]R_1[/latex] (letting [latex]P_3[/latex]'s wait resolve), and removing [latex]P_4[/latex] frees [latex]R_4[/latex] (letting [latex]P_2[/latex]'s wait for [latex]R_4[/latex] resolve); with both freed, the remaining chain ([latex]P_2,P_3[/latex]) can fully unwind — deadlock-free.

Answer: Aborting P2 alone works; and aborting both P1 and P4 together works.

Click here for detail solution
options: Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
Aborting [latex]P_3 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
Aborting [latex]P_2 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] and [latex]P_4 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.

questions.text:
Consider a demand paging system with three frames, and the following page reference string: 1 2 3 4 5 4 1 6 4 5 1 3 2. The contents of the frames are as follows initially and after each reference (from left to right):

The *-marked references cause page replacements.
Which one or more of the following could be the page replacement policy/policies in use?
questions.solution:
Working through the given frame-content trace and testing it against each replacement policy's actual decision rule at every fault:

At the point where a page must be evicted, the trace consistently evicts whichever current page is used farthest in the future (or never again) — exactly matching the Optimal page replacement policy's defining rule.

Checking this same trace against LRU's rule (evict the least-recently-used) gives a different eviction choice at at least one fault point; checking against LFU's rule (evict least-frequently-used so far) also disagrees with the trace at some point; and MFU's rule (evict the most-frequently-used) likewise contradicts the trace elsewhere. Only Optimal's rule is consistent with every single eviction decision shown.

Answer: Optimal page replacement policy

questions.text:
Processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 [/latex] arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling policy. Ignore context switching times.
Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four processes in milliseconds?
questions.solution:
Simulate SRTF (always run whichever available process has the least remaining time):

[latex]t{=}0[/latex]: only [latex]P_1[/latex] present (remaining [latex]10[/latex]) → runs.
[latex]t{=}1[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]13[/latex]); [latex]P_1[/latex]'s remaining ([latex]9[/latex]) is still shortest → [latex]P_1[/latex] continues.
[latex]t{=}2[/latex]: [latex]P_3[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]6[/latex]); now shortest among [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_3[/latex]([latex]6[/latex]) is [latex]P_3[/latex] → switch to [latex]P_3[/latex].
[latex]P_3[/latex] runs uninterrupted [latex]t{=}2[/latex] to [latex]t{=}8[/latex] (no shorter arrivals in between), finishing exactly as [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives. [latex]P_3[/latex] turnaround [latex]=8-2=6[/latex].
[latex]t{=}8[/latex]: [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]9[/latex]); comparing [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_1[/latex] shortest, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}16[/latex]. [latex]P_1[/latex] turnaround [latex]=16-0=16[/latex].
[latex]t{=}16[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]) vs [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_4[/latex] runs to completion at [latex]t{=}25[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=25-8=17[/latex].
[latex]t{=}25[/latex]: only [latex]P_2[/latex] left, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}38[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=38-1=37[/latex].

Average turnaround [latex]=\dfrac{6+16+17+37}4=\dfrac{76}4=19[/latex]

Answer: 19

questions.text:
In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page replacement algorithm is as follows:
The OS correctly predicts only up to next 4 page references (including the current page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.
A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:

1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4.

If the system has three memory frames that are initially empty, the number of page faults that will occur during execution of the process is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.solution:
With the OS able to correctly predict only the next [latex]4[/latex] references (including the current one) at the moment a frame is allocated, simulate the reference string [latex]1,3,2,4,2,3,1,2,4,3,1,4[/latex] with [latex]3[/latex] initially-empty frames:

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Ref}&\text{Frames after}&\text{Fault?}\\\hline1&\{1\}&\text{Fault}\\3&\{1,3\}&\text{Fault}\\2&\{1,3,2\}&\text{Fault}\\4&\{4,3,2\}\ (\text{evict }1\text{, unused within next window }2,3,1)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\1&\{4,2,1\}\ (\text{evict }3\text{, farthest-future within window }2,4,3)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,1,3\}\ (\text{evict }2\text{, no longer used in remaining string})&\text{Fault}\\1&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\end{array}[/latex]

Total page faults [latex]=6[/latex] (at references [latex]1,3,2,4,1,3[/latex] in the sequence, marked "Fault" above).

Answer: 6

questions.text: A disk of size [latex] 512M [/latex] bytes is divided into blocks of [latex] 64K [/latex] bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. Each data block reserves 4 bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of [latex] 1M [/latex] bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, [latex] 1K=2^{10}, 1M=2^{20} [/latex]. The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.solution:
Disk block size [latex]=64K=2^{16}[/latex] bytes. In linked allocation, every block (including the last) reserves [latex]4[/latex] bytes for its "next" pointer field, leaving usable data capacity per block [latex]=65536-4=65532[/latex] bytes.

File size [latex]=1M=2^{20}=1{,}048{,}576[/latex] bytes. Number of blocks needed [latex]=\lceil1{,}048{,}576/65532\rceil[/latex]: since [latex]65532\times16=1{,}048{,}512[/latex] (short of the file size by [latex]64[/latex] bytes), a [latex]17[/latex]th block is required, giving [latex]17[/latex] blocks total.

Total disk space allocated [latex]=17\times65536=1{,}114{,}112[/latex] bytes. Space genuinely "useful" (actual file data plus the [latex]4[/latex]-byte pointer overhead in each of the [latex]17[/latex] blocks) [latex]=1{,}048{,}576+17\times4=1{,}048{,}576+68=1{,}048{,}644[/latex] bytes.

Internal fragmentation (wasted space) [latex]=1{,}114{,}112-1{,}048{,}644=65{,}468[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 65468
